Are we making young lawyers work too hard?

I’ve been asking myself this question lately.

Not because I think young lawyers shouldn’t work hard. They should. I did, and I still believe that there is no substitute for putting in the work, particularly in the early years of a career.

But I wonder whether, somewhere along the way, we have started to equate commitment to the profession with giving the profession more and more of our time.

I have spent most of my working life in the legal profession, and today, as Managing Partner of Poovayya & Co., I find myself thinking about this from a slightly different perspective.

We have a responsibility not only to train good lawyers, but also to think about the kind of professional lives we are helping them build.

And that makes me wonder how much space the law should really occupy in a young person’s life.

At some point, I think we need to recognise that being a lawyer is only one part of who we are.

We have other interests, relationships, passions and curiosities that deserve some attention too.

And I don’t think those things necessarily take away from our professional lives. In many ways, they enrich them.

Some of the things I have learnt outside the law-through sport, travel, founding businesses, community projects and simply meeting people from completely different walks of life - have shaped the way I think as a lawyer and as a leader.

Which makes me wonder whether we should be thinking less about how many hours young lawyers are putting in and more about how effectively they are using those hours.

There will always be periods when the job demands more. That is the nature of our profession.

But should the expectation be that a young lawyer’s life revolves around the law?

I’m not sure it should.

Perhaps we should be building a profession where people can work hard, become very good at what they do, build successful careers and still have the time and energy to discover who they are outside the profession.

After all, we are not just lawyers.

We happen to practise law.

There is a difference.
Poovayya & Co.
